planting.note: Set out container-grown trees only after nighttime lows are reliably above 50°F and give young trees a sheltered, warm microclimate.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil enriched with compost, choosing the warmest and most wind-protected spot available since this tree resents any chill below the mid-40s. Keep the root zone consistently moist during establishment and expect a large, glossy-leaved tree that eventually bears heavy, applesauce-scented fruit with a pale, custard-like pulp. On the Gulf Coast it is realistically grown only in the warmest coastal pockets of south Florida or in a large container that can be moved into a greenhouse for winter. Young trees should be protected from any frost, as even brief freezes can kill wood back to the ground.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Plant Records

planting.note: Move container plants outdoors only once nights stay above 55°F, and bring them under cover well before the first fall cold front.

directions: Grow this understory shrub from the Colombian Chocó rainforest in a large pot of rich, moisture-retentive potting mix, since it wants filtered light and constant humidity rather than harsh full sun. It produces large, dense, brown fruits packed with a thick, tart pulp that is almost always processed into juice or preserves rather than eaten fresh. Because it is one of the most cold-sensitive fruiting plants grown by tropical fruit collectors, Gulf Coast and Florida growers keep it strictly as a greenhouse or sunroom container specimen and never leave it outside once temperatures dip toward 50°F. Consistent watering and high humidity are more important to fruit set than any particular soil type.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Plant Records

planting.note: Root stem cuttings and set out against a sturdy trellis or post once all danger of frost has passed.

directions: Propagate from mature stem cuttings and train the sprawling, three-angled stems onto a stout trellis in full sun with sharply draining soil, since standing water quickly rots the succulent growth. This white-fleshed cultivar is prized among collectors for consistently sweet, well-balanced flavor compared with many bland commercial dragon fruit. Gulf Coast growers keep it in large pots so it can be wheeled under cover whenever temperatures threaten to drop into the 30s, since the stems are more cold-tender than typical landscape cactus. Hand-pollination in the evening, when the large white flowers open, improves fruit set for home growers.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension
California Rare Fruit Growers

planting.note: Root stem cuttings and transplant to a sturdy support once nighttime lows are reliably above 50°F.

directions: Grow from cuttings taken from a healthy mother plant and support the vining stems on a post or arbor in full sun with fast-draining, cactus-style soil. This deep magenta-red-fleshed selection is grown by home collectors specifically for its intensely colored, richly flavored fruit, which stands out from the milder white-fleshed types. Because the succulent stems are damaged by hard freezes, Gulf Coast growers generally keep it container-grown so it can be moved to a garage or greenhouse whenever a freeze warning is issued. Fruit set improves with hand pollination shortly after the night-blooming flowers open, since many dragon fruit types are only partially self-fertile.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension
California Rare Fruit Growers

planting.note: Transplant grafted trees into the landscape or a large container after the last frost, once soil has warmed.

directions: Plant a grafted specimen in well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, choosing a warm, sheltered site out of harsh drying winds since young leaves are sensitive to cold snaps. This widely grown Thai-origin selection produces heavy clusters of sweet, low-acid, deeply ribbed fruit and tends to bear more prolifically than seedling carambola trees. Because established wood can suffer damage below the upper 20s, Gulf Coast growers plant it in the warmest microclimate on the property or keep smaller trees in containers that can be moved under cover during freezes. Regular irrigation through fruit development produces juicier, less fibrous fruit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
Rare Fruit Council International

planting.note: Set out grafted trees in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has passed and soil has warmed thoroughly.

directions: Grow this Cuban-origin, grafted mamey sapote cultivar in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing plenty of room for a large, long-lived tree. It is valued by south Florida growers for reliably producing smooth-skinned fruit with dense, sweet, salmon-pink flesh often compared to sweet potato or pumpkin custard. Young trees are noticeably cold-tender and can lose leaves or twigs at temperatures in the mid-30s, so Gulf Coast growers stick to the warmest coastal locations or grow smaller trees in large containers that come indoors for winter. Mature trees take several years to bear their first crop, and fruit is harvested firm and then ripened off the tree at room temperature.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Plant Records

planting.note: Transplant grafted or rooted trees into full sun once nights stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving this compact-growing selection room to branch out into a small, rounded tree. Unlike typical seedy sugar apples, this cultivar sets fruit that are largely seedless or nearly so, with the same custardy, sweet, segmented flesh that makes the species popular across south Florida dooryards. It defoliates in cool weather and is killed back by hard frost, so Gulf Coast growers favor sheltered south-facing walls or grow young trees in containers that can be moved into a garage during freezes. Hand pollination with a small brush in the early morning often improves fruit set, since natural pollinators can be scarce in home gardens.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Plant Records

planting.note: Set out grafted trees in a warm, sunny, wind-protected site once frost risk has fully passed.

directions: Grow this heavy-bearing grafted sapodilla cultivar in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing it well away from structures since mature trees become quite large and dense. It is grown commercially in south Florida for producing abundant crops of medium-sized fruit with grainy, malt-and-brown-sugar-flavored flesh once fully ripened off the tree. Established trees tolerate brief light frost better than many tropical fruits but still suffer leaf and twig damage below the upper 20s, so Gulf Coast growers reserve it for the warmest zones or keep young trees containerized for winter protection. Fruit must soften fully before eating, as unripe sapodilla is astringent with latex.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
Rare Fruit Council International

planting.note: Transplant grafted air-layered trees into acidic, well-drained soil after the last frost, in a sunny sheltered spot.

directions: Plant an air-layered or grafted tree in acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, choosing a sunny site protected from strong wind. This cultivar is grown for its unusually large, thin-shelled fruit with sweet, juicy flesh and a smaller seed than many other lychee selections. Established trees handle brief dips into the upper 20s better than young trees but still benefit from overhead frost protection or covering during hard freezes on the Gulf Coast. Lychees need a period of cool, dry weather to initiate flowering, which makes fruiting inconsistent in the humid Gulf South even though the trees themselves can be grown successfully.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost.

directions: Train this vigorous, purple-fruited passion vine onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, watering deeply during dry spells to keep production steady. It is grown for its noticeably better cold tolerance than typical yellow passion fruit selections, often resprouting from the root crown after the top growth is cut back by a freeze. On the Gulf Coast growers mulch the root zone heavily going into winter and treat the vine as a root-hardy perennial that regrows each spring even where hard freezes are common. Ripe fruit, which drops naturally from the vine, has an intensely aromatic, tart-sweet pulp used fresh or for juice.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension
